title: How to sustain journalism that rarely pays for itself
content:
Investigative journalism is expensive to produce and rarely pays for itself. A single story can require months of reporting, cross-border collaboration, specialist expertise and legal support, with no guarantee that the revenue it generates will cover those costs. For newsrooms doing this work, financial sustainability means finding ways to sustain reporting whose public value far exceeds its commercial return.

That makes decisions about revenue especially consequential. Time spent developing a new income stream is time a small team cannot spend investigating. Yet dependence on a narrow funding base can leave a newsroom vulnerable to shifting donor priorities or pressure from advertisers. The challenge is to identify sources of income that fit an organisation’s editorial mission, make sensible use of its limited resources and protect its independence.

title: Cross-border journalism comes to Budapest
content:
Investigative journalists from across Europe and beyond gathered in the Hungarian capital on September 17 and 18 for UNCOVERED 2026, the annual conference of the Investigative Journalism for Europe (IJ4EU) programme. The event brought together reporters, editors and media experts to examine the pressures facing cross-border journalism and the practical challenges of doing it.

Around 150 participants from 32 countries attended the sixth edition of the conference, hosted by Goethe-Institut Hungary, for a day and a half of panels, workshops, mentoring and exchanges on subjects ranging from government pressure and journalist safety to newsroom sustainability, freelance working conditions and the impact of major investigations.

At the centre of the programme was a question that ran through much of the conference: how can investigative journalists work across borders, withstand mounting political and financial pressure, and produce reporting that leads to meaningful change?

Here is a brief recap of UNCOVERED 2026, told through pictures.

title: Beyond publication: How watchdog journalism makes a difference
content:
What do the 2026 IJ4EU Impact Awards reveal about the ambitions, pressures and responsibilities of investigative journalism in Europe?

A doctor sanctioned in one country resumes practising in another. A chemical factory closes in Europe, only to reappear thousands of kilometres away. Industry lobbying shapes a regulatory debate with little public scrutiny. A photograph celebrated by journalism’s own institutions carries a false description of a murdered man for three decades.

The investigations recognised at IJ4EU’s 2026 Impact Awards exposed very different failures. Taken together, they offer a revealing picture of the work independent investigative journalism is being asked to do: follow problems beyond the boundaries of national oversight, test the claims of powerful interests and dig into uncomfortable truths.

They also raise a question that extends well beyond an awards ceremony. What should count as evidence that this work matters?

“Our discussions kept returning to one deceptively simple question,” said jury chair Leila Bičakčić, co-founder and executive director of the Center for Investigative Reporting in Sarajevo. “What do we mean when we say that journalism has impact?”

title: Why journalism grants can put freelancers at a disadvantage
content:
When Romanian investigative journalist Andrei Petre began researching secrecy surrounding European data centres in 2025, he had documents, a story idea and, eventually, an interested publisher.

What he didn’t have was funding.

Petre applied for a journalism grant but was rejected because his preliminary research was judged insufficient. He continued researching and applied again.

While he waited, another investigative team published a story based on one of the key public documents he had found. His prospective publishing partner was subsequently approached to join that investigation instead. Petre did not get the grant.

His experience illustrated a dilemma at the heart of “The Uneven Split”, a panel debate at IJ4EU’s 2026 UNCOVERED Conference in Budapest: freelancers may need to undertake substantial unpaid reporting to secure funding, but waiting for that funding can mean losing a fast-moving story.

“You cannot really cover stuff that other people are already covering because you have to wait a lot until you get a grant,” Petre said.

title: Why investigative teams fall into conflict — and what to do about it
content:
A room full of investigative journalists closed their eyes, took a sheet of A4 paper and followed a set of instructions. Fold it in half. Tear off the upper right corner. Fold it again. Tear off the lower right corner. No questions were allowed.

When they opened their eyes and unfolded the paper, the results were markedly different. Some had intricate patterns. Others were little more than shredded paper.

For Emma Thomasson, who was leading a workshop on communication and conflict at IJ4EU’s UNCOVERED Conference in Budapest, the exercise illustrated a basic problem in collaborative work: giving people the same instructions does not mean they will understand them in the same way.

“The point here is that communication is difficult, and particularly difficult if we are not all from the same background,” said Thomasson, a former Reuters bureau chief who now offers training and consulting on leadership, communication, innovation and workplace wellbeing.

title: IJ4EU Impact Award 2026 winners announced
content:
Two investigations into deadly “forever chemicals” are among the three winners of the 2026 IJ4EU Impact Awards, alongside a cross-border exposé showing how doctors sanctioned for malpractice are able to continue working after being banned elsewhere.

The winning teams of journalists each received €5,000 at the annual awards presented by the Investigative Journalism for Europe (IJ4EU) fund, which supports cross-border public-interest journalism in Europe.

In alphabetical order, the three equal winners are:

  • Bad Practice, by a consortium of 50 media outlets led by OCCRP, VG and The Times.
  • Factories on the Run: Inside the Global Trade that Moves PFAS Downstream, by Gianluca Liva, Marta Frigerio, Anna Violato, Filippo Tommasoli, Thomas Goorden and Varrun Sukhraj.
  • The Forever Lobbying Project, by a consortium of European media partners coordinated by Le Monde.

    • The jury also singled out Killing for the Photo, by Barbara Matejčić in collaboration with Natalija Jovanović and Ruben Brugnera, for special recognition.

    The winners were announced on September 17 in Budapest at IJ4EU’s annual UNCOVERED Conference, hosted this year by Goethe-Institut Hungary.

title: Jury unveiled for IJ4EU Impact Awards 2026
content:
The European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF), a partner in the IJ4EU fund, has unveiled the identities of the jury members presiding over the IJ4EU Impact Awards 2026.

Chaired by Bosnian investigative journalism leader Leila Bičakčić, the jury has chosen three equal winners, each of whom will receive a €5,000 cash prize in recognition of outstanding cross-border investigative journalism in Europe.

The winners will be announced in Budapest on September 17 during UNCOVERED 2026, the latest edition of IJ4EU’s annual conference bringing together investigative journalists, editors, media organisations and supporters of public-interest journalism from across Europe.

UNCOVERED is organised by ECPMF in partnership with the International Press Institute and the European Journalism Centre, its partners in the Investigative Journalism for Europe (IJ4EU) programme.

Here are profiles of the Impact Award jury members.

title: IJ4EU UNCOVERED 2026: What’s on the agenda?
content:
The agenda for UNCOVERED 2026 is officially live!

From panels and keynotes on what makes investigative journalism matter and what makes it survive, to practical workshops, this year’s lineup is one of our fullest yet.

Some of our favourites from past editions are back as well: Expect three Cross-Border Snapshot sessions featuring IJ4EU’s current grantees, one-on-one Power Chats with experienced mentors to talk about finances, coordinating collaborations, satellite journalism, or reporting on environmental crises, and of course, the IJ4EU Impact Award Ceremony, where the most impactful stories of 2025, as selected by an independent jury, will be revealed. See the shortlisted entries here.

And there is always more to UNCOVERED: an open mic, a trivia quiz, and a chance to connect, swap stories, and maybe meet your next project partners.

Explore the full agenda and meet the speakers.

title: Ten investigations shortlisted for IJ4EU Impact Awards 2026
content:
Ten outstanding investigations have been shortlisted for the 2026 IJ4EU Impact Awards, celebrating collaborative journalism that drives real change across borders in Europe.

With a record 50 eligible entries this year, the nominations reflect cross-border collaboration in European watchdog journalism at its strongest yet. The nominated teams comprise nearly 600 journalists from 63 countries, including 26 EU member states, and span a geographical range from Iceland to Uganda.

Independent evaluators at Leipzig University carried out the pre-evaluation process that produced the shortlist. The process was convened by the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF), one of the IJ4EU fund’s core partners. 

Three winning teams, each receiving €5,000, will be chosen by an independent jury chaired by Leila Bičakčić, one of Southeast Europe’s leading investigative journalism experts. The jury will consider all eligible nominations in reaching its final decision.

The winners will be announced on September 17, 2026 during IJ4EU’s annual UNCOVERED Conference, hosted in Budapest by Goethe-Institut Hungary.

title: Leila Bičakčić to chair IJ4EU Impact Award jury
content:
Leila Bičakčić, one of Southeast Europe’s leading investigative journalism and media development experts, will chair the jury for the 2026 edition of the IJ4EU Impact Awards.

Bičakčić is co-founder and executive director of the Center for Investigative Reporting (CIN) in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Over more than two decades, she has helped build CIN into one of foremost investigative newsrooms in the Balkans, overseeing major investigations into corruption, organised crime, judicial accountability, and public governance.

Under her leadership, CIN has earned a reputation for rigorous, evidence-based reporting that has informed public debate, prompted institutional reforms, and strengthened public accountability.

Beyond the newsroom, Bičakčić has played an important role in advancing investigative journalism across the Western Balkans. She has mentored journalists, led regional media development initiatives, built international partnerships, and served on grant-selection and evaluation panels supporting independent journalism and civil society.
